findings.text: test_readmelockrow_theemptinessclaim_matchesthefilecontents calls cfg.set_password('prod','pw') after isolate_config, which redirects only XDG_CONFIG_HOME and never calls install_fake_keychain. Every successful run writes a real entry into the machine's OS keychain under redshift-comment-mcp/prod and the probe's outcome depends on real keychain state. Verified contained: the other three keychain-touching probes stub correctly and two never touch it. Not fixed here because Round 3 is the episode's terminal digest and the file is the adversary's artifact.

The report claims the keychain entry's timestamp predates the verification run and therefore was not caused by it. That reasoning is unsound: the macOS keyring backend's set_password deletes then re-adds, resetting cdat as well as mdat, so a timestamp cannot establish causation either way. What is established is that every successful run of the probe above rewrites the entry. Uncorrectable within this episode; recorded so the permanent record is not left with the weaker claim.
Deleting the config directory itself mid-write defeats both locks. The retry catches a directory replaced between open and flock, not one removed while held.
The re-entrancy counter is process-local, so a fork() while the lock is held would carry a non-zero depth into the child. No caller forks inside a write.
Calls keyring.get_password(KEYRING_SERVICE, name) directly rather than the module's own get_password(name) wrapper, duplicating a one-line body. Below Rule of Three.
Plan risk 5: with the write atomic, the write_profile_failed rollback can only revert another process's completed write. Deferred to 2026-09-17-credential-resolution-hardening, which owns that file.
The Data line cites config.py:86 for the whole-table replace; at the base commit that line is the in-memory mutation and the replace is at :87-88.
